title: Building ShieldSigner with AI
subtitle: How AI helped design a PCB, model a case and bring a tiny Linux signer to life.

slides.title: Building ShieldSigner with AI
slides.summary: From schematic to printable enclosure, driven by code.
points: PCB → assembly → enclosure
Fast iteration. Explicit evidence.
slides.notes: This is a builder story: using AI to move between schematics, source, supplier drawings and mechanical models. The project is a development prototype, not a claim that a home-built signer is safer than commercial products. The main story is the PCB and 3D iteration; the camera and LVGL work show what happened when the hardware met software. Credit SeedSigner, ShieldSigner and their contributors throughout.

slides.title: What does a Bitcoin signer do?
slides.summary: Review a proposed transaction. Approve a signature.
points: The coordinator prepares the transaction
The signer displays the transaction details, then signs it after you approve
The coordinator broadcasts the result
slides.notes: Start without assuming Bitcoin expertise. Coins are recorded on the network; the device holds or temporarily reconstructs keys that authorize spending. PSBT means partially signed Bitcoin transaction: a package of transaction data and signing metadata. The coordinator can prepare a proposal without having the private keys. The signer must show meaningful outputs and fees for the human to verify. SeedSigner exchanges this information through QR codes; the coordinator then collects signatures and broadcasts. A QR air gap changes the transport, but untrusted inputs and misleading transaction information still need validation. A seed is a backup secret, not a picture to project during this talk.

slides.title: From SeedSigner to ShieldSigner
slides.summary: What we inherited, adapted and built.
points: SeedSigner: Python signing application
ShieldSigner: Luckfox and smartcard adaptations
This project: carrier, case and integration
slides.notes: Credit the lineage before discussing AI. SeedSigner provides the original application, QR workflow and Raspberry Pi hardware ecosystem. ShieldSigner adapts the project toward Luckfox and smartcards. Our work builds on those contributors, the pinned application and kdmukai’s portable LVGL screens. The custom 2.8-inch pill carrier and enclosure are new design work; the demonstrated device is the existing 240×240 bench. Distinguish reuse, adaptation and original integration. AI helped navigate these boundaries and build repeatable tools; it did not invent the Bitcoin protocol or replace the upstream signing implementation.

slides.title: Where trust enters the system
slides.summary: Keys, software, hardware, distribution and recovery.
points: Seed generation
Device + distribution
Recovery + verification
slides.notes: Before showing CAD, explain the motivation: understand the interfaces and reduce opaque assumptions. Firmware, entropy generation, the device, reseller handling, coordinator and backups are different trust boundaries. Open source helps inspection; it does not prove a particular binary, assembled board or recovery procedure is correct. Building this prototype teaches those boundaries rather than removing them.

slides.title: Two hardware-wallet incidents
slides.summary: Different failures in seed generation and device distribution.
points: July: weakened seed generation
October: reseller hardware implants
Updating ≠ repairing an old seed
slides.notes: Coinkite published its seed-generation advisory on July 30, 2026. Affected firmware produced weakened seeds; its current status page distinguishes fixed releases and explains that updating does not repair an already affected seed. Check the official guidance rather than a model-name shortcut. Ledger’s October 15 response describes localized reseller-distribution implants that captured recovery phrases during setup. Ledger says its chip, OS and servers were not compromised. These illustrate distinct failure paths, not proof that either whole product family or our prototype is categorically unsafe or safe. Do not state unverified aggregate theft figures.

slides.title: Multi-vendor multisig
slides.summary: An experimental signer can participate without controlling the wallet.
points: Spread trust across vendors and implementations
One compromised signer cannot spend on its own
Keep a recovery path without the experimental device
slides.notes: The audience already understands the threshold; spend this slide on why the signers should differ. A hypothetical 2-of-3 arrangement can combine two established signers from different vendors with an experimental ShieldSigner, each holding an independently generated key. If only the experimental key is exposed, it cannot authorize a spend. If the prototype is unavailable, the other two can still sign, provided they remain available and the wallet configuration is retained. Compared with placing sole authority in that experimental device, this limits the consequences of its failure or compromise. It is not a blanket claim that any multisig arrangement is safer than every single-signer setup: correlated dependencies, compromised wallet setup, misleading addresses, operational mistakes and backup loss still matter. Verify the policy and receive/change addresses using independently trusted devices, review transactions there, retain the descriptor and test recovery. Vendor names alone do not establish implementation independence; the following library slide explains shared dependencies. This is an architecture argument, not a report of a qualified or funded ShieldSigner deployment. The next step for this prototype is practice with disposable keys and every signing pair, not assigning it sole custody.

slides.title: The SeedSigner software stack
slides.summary: How the application, libraries, UI and drivers fit together.
points: Application policy stays above the libraries
Bitcoin parsing and cryptography are different layers
UI, QR and drivers have their own interfaces
slides.notes: Follow the three branches from the application: Bitcoin data and signing, camera and QR input, and screen rendering and user input. embit handles Bitcoin structures and operations; its cryptographic backend performs lower-level curve operations. QR readers supply decoded data to the application. Linux and board drivers support all hardware-facing services. The diagram describes responsibilities and connections; the dedicated camera and UI sections explain our implementations.

blocks.title: embit
blocks.role: Provides Bitcoin transaction, PSBT, descriptor and key-handling functions.
blocks.connection: The application calls embit to interpret Bitcoin data, derive keys and create signatures.

blocks.title: Cryptographic backend
blocks.role: Performs the low-level elliptic-curve operations used for public keys and signatures.
blocks.connection: embit calls a cryptographic backend selected for its runtime environment.

blocks.title: QR and animated formats
blocks.role: Reads QR codes and assembles animated sequences into a complete payload.
blocks.connection: Camera frames go to the QR decoder; decoded bytes go to the application’s format handlers.

blocks.title: Camera acquisition
blocks.role: Captures images for the preview and QR scanning.
blocks.connection: Sensor and ISP drivers provide frames to the camera service, which passes them to the preview and QR decoder.

blocks.title: Screen rendering
blocks.role: Draws menus, transaction details and QR codes.
blocks.connection: The application sends screen content to the renderer and receives selections and actions in return.

blocks.title: Display and input I/O
blocks.role: Sends pixels to the display and reads button presses.
blocks.connection: Display drivers use SPI and control GPIOs; input drivers turn switch signals into application events.

slides.caption: Parallel branches serve the application. The cryptographic backend sits beneath the Bitcoin library; QR decoding does not replace transaction parsing.
slides.hubRole: Coordinates navigation, wallet state, transaction review and signing.
slides.hubConnection: Calls the Bitcoin library, QR handlers and screen services to carry out the user’s chosen workflow.
slides.foundationRole: CPython executes the application. Linux manages processes, memory and access to devices.
slides.foundationConnection: Board-specific drivers connect the software services to the camera, display and GPIO hardware.

slides.title: Bitcoin libraries and shared dependencies
slides.summary: embit, rust-bitcoin and libwally take different approaches.
points: embit · rust-bitcoin · libwally
APIs and supported features differ
Shared dependencies need explicit review
slides.notes: Explain the distinction between a Bitcoin library and a primitive cryptography implementation. embit targets embedded Python/MicroPython applications. rust-bitcoin provides Rust Bitcoin types and serialization. libwally offers C wallet primitives and bindings. These are examples to compare, not three installed alternatives in this firmware and not drop-in replacements. embit can select a libsecp256k1-based backend; libwally includes libsecp sources, and the Rust ecosystem also has secp256k1 bindings. Different languages therefore do not establish independent cryptographic ancestry. Reuse can concentrate expert review and fixes; independent implementations can reduce some common failure modes but require serious testing. An adapter should compare descriptor/address derivation, transaction round trips, signing preimages, valid signatures, and malformed or unsupported inputs. Matching test vectors do not prove complete independence or correctness.

slides.title: The hardware and its connections
slides.summary: From the Raspberry Pi reference build to our Luckfox carrier.
points: A connector shape is not a pinout
Bus, voltage and geometry must agree
A new processor is a board + software port
slides.notes: Follow each connection from the Luckfox Mini. The camera uses the module camera connector. The display uses SPI and control GPIOs; the switches use GPIO inputs. UART connects the SEC1210 smartcard controller to the host, while the controller manages card contacts. The carrier routes power and signals, and the enclosure positions the parts. USB-C is a power input. Use one 5 V power source at a time.
slides.hubDetail: Our adaptation: Luckfox Mini + microSD boot on a custom 160 × 70 mm carrier

blocks.title: Camera
blocks.connection: The SC3336 camera connects to the Luckfox module’s dedicated camera connector and feeds its image-processing pipeline.

blocks.title: Display
blocks.role: Shows menus, transaction details and QR codes.
blocks.connection: The eight-pin HOTHMI module receives pixels over SPI, with GPIO signals for command selection and reset.

blocks.title: Controls
blocks.role: Lets the user navigate, select and confirm actions.
blocks.connection: Joystick directions, joystick press and three keys connect to GPIO inputs with pull-ups.

blocks.title: Smartcard
blocks.role: Provides a contact interface for supported smartcards.
blocks.connection: The Luckfox communicates over UART with the SEC1210, which handles card power, clock, reset and data through the socket.

blocks.title: Power
blocks.role: Supplies power to the compute module and carrier electronics.
blocks.connection: USB-C or the two-pin header supplies 5 V; a dedicated regulator supplies the display’s 3.3 V rail. USB-C is power-only.

blocks.title: Carrier and enclosure
blocks.role: Routes the electrical connections and holds the assembly in place.
blocks.connection: PCB headers join the modules; enclosure mounts and spacers position the board, display, controls and camera.

slides.caption: These are functional connections, not a wiring diagram. Camera connects to the compute module; the carrier routes the display, controls, power and card interface.

slides.title: Replacing hardware and software
slides.summary: What can change, and what needs to stay compatible.
points: LVGL: a demonstrated screen boundary
New LCD: driver + wiring + mechanical work
New Bitcoin library: semantic compatibility work
slides.notes: Use these three contrasting examples. The LVGL migration demonstrates a replacement through a defined screen/event protocol while preserving the original application’s decisions. A new LCD has a familiar SPI bus but can differ in numbering, controller initialization, dimensions and electrical requirements. Replacing embit is deeper: the adapter must preserve wallet semantics, not just function names. The capability diagram shows possibilities; it does not claim every block has been replaced. Distinguish the working bench, native software checks and unqualified pill first article throughout.

slides.title: How I worked with AI
slides.summary: I set the direction. AI helped turn it into code, tools and working hardware.
points: Start with a concrete change
Keep the result easy to inspect
Turn repeated work into tools
slides.notes: My role was to choose the goals, constraints and tradeoffs, then inspect the results and test the hardware. AI helped read repositories and datasheets, trace connections, edit PCB and enclosure files, port software and write the tools to repeat those edits. The silkscreen example is small enough to follow end to end: start with official artwork, generate native KiCad polygons, render the board and check that the electrical design stayed unchanged. The same pattern scales to moving components, changing case dimensions and iterating camera software. Independent research and review can run in parallel; changes still need clear ownership. When the process wandered, a smaller task and an explicit next test brought it back. Each useful iteration left behind source, a repeatable command and evidence I could review. On the camera and UI, that included running the result on the real board.

slides.title: Designing the carrier PCB
slides.summary: AI helped connect datasheet research, electrical review and repeatable manufacturing outputs.
points: Read the datasheets for every major IC and module
Match KiCad symbol pins and footprint pads to the real part
Check voltage domains, signal functions and connector order
Generate matched BOM, placement, Gerber and drill files
slides.notes: Start by collecting the manufacturer datasheets and mechanical drawings for the major components: the Luckfox module, LCD, camera, smartcard controller, regulators and connectors. AI helps extract pin tables, supply limits, interface requirements and recommended support circuitry into a reviewable component guide. Check each KiCad symbol pin number, name and electrical type against the datasheet, then follow it through the footprint pad and board net to the physical part. Check connector viewing direction and pin-one orientation as well as signal names. This caught concrete issues: SEC1210 power-output pin types needed correcting, and its output decoupling changed from 100 nF to 1 µF to match the datasheet recommendation. Review voltage domains, module pinmux, bus signals and power paths together. Use scripts for repeatable native edits, then run schematic ERC, PCB DRC, connectivity and schematic-to-PCB parity checks. Generate the BOM with readable values, manufacturer part numbers and supplier references, the CPL pick-and-place file, and Gerbers and drill files from the same revision. Keep DNP choices and assembly rotations explicit. The main review kit has 35 fitted SMT parts across 17 supplier SKUs. Automated checks and a manufacturing package still require a physical first article to qualify assembly, fit and powered operation.

slides.title: Porting the board to tscircuit
slides.summary: TypeScript could make tscircuit a more AI-native PCB tool in the future. I still prefer KiCad today.
points: Components and connections expressed in TypeScript
Seven sheets, editable silk and 3D models
Check footprints and electrical connections
slides.notes: Show a concrete AI iteration: the first port reproduced appearance using imported native geometry and copper, which was useful for comparison but not idiomatic source authoring. The rebuilt version uses semantic tscircuit primitives, functional sheets, local footprints and assets, and fresh built-in autorouting. Compare 190 physical lands within 0.005 mm and electrical partitions in both directions, then run placement, shorts and routing-style checks. That establishes specific software evidence, not hardware qualification or equal routed copper. This example demonstrates tool translation; KiCad remains the native reference and preferred workflow. There are recorded upstream core/schema incompatibilities and unresolved generic-header part-selection warnings; do not claim a perfect exporter or production-ready new layout. The longer-term possibility is a more AI-native PCB workflow: components, connections and layout are expressed in TypeScript, giving AI familiar source code to read, edit and review with normal diffs. That is a promising direction rather than a claim that tscircuit is already a more mature PCB editor.

slides.title: Designing the enclosure in OpenSCAD
slides.summary: OpenSCAD creates 3D models from code: shapes, dimensions and operations.
points: Combine shapes; subtract holes and openings
Use parameters for walls, clearances and mounting posts
Change the code, preview the model, export parts to print
slides.notes: OpenSCAD is a code-based 3D CAD tool. You describe solids such as boxes and cylinders, position them with transforms, and combine or subtract them. A case wall can begin as an outer box with an inner box removed; another cut creates a connector opening. Variables and reusable modules control dimensions and repeated features such as screw posts. Preview the model as you edit, then render and export a mesh for slicing and printing. This gives AI concrete source code to work with and gives us readable diffs and repeatable geometry. For this project, the PCB supplies the outline, mounting holes and component positions; module drawings supply the remaining dimensions. Adjust the case around those constraints, then inspect the complete assembly in the next section. Camera and ribbon models are adjustable envelopes and screw threads are omitted.

slides.title: Does the complete assembly fit?
slides.summary: Bring the PCB, modules and enclosure together to inspect the fit.
points: Inspect header heights and mating depths
Look for collisions and blocked connectors
Use the model to plan a printed fit test
slides.notes: Now inspect the result of the PCB and enclosure work together. Rotate the assembled model, open the exploded view, and use PCB assembly and transparent case-fit modes to inspect interfaces. Check that display and Luckfox headers mate at the intended depth, spacers support the stack, and connectors and buttons remain accessible. Look at camera placement and cable clearance. If a header makes the case too thick or an opening is blocked, return to the PCB or case parameters and regenerate. A digital model helps identify problems before printing; a printed fit sample and real purchased components are still needed to verify tolerances. Finish the hardware story here, then move on to the camera and UI software.

slides.title: Controlling the camera in Rust
slides.summary: AI helped investigate the vendor interfaces and build a camera service we could inspect and change.
points: Trace sensor and image-processing controls
Implement exposure, white balance and frame delivery
Inspect captures and test each change on hardware
slides.notes: Bridge from physical fit to software: even with the camera connected, the application needs correctly exposed frames it can decode. AI helped investigate the vendor interfaces, implement a Rust camera service and iterate against images and QR tests on the real camera. The useful loop was inspect a capture, identify a specific problem, change the implementation and test again. Exposure, white balance and the frame path mattered more than a successful build. The service uses existing Linux sensor and ISP drivers without calling the RKAIQ userspace library; this is not complete RKAIQ parity or a Linux-free design. ZXing-C++ is the existing QR decoder. It consumes grayscale frames directly, avoiding an unnecessary JPEG conversion, and returns bytes for the Python application to assemble and interpret. The next section addresses how the application displays its interface. Keep QR decoder selection for the next slide: this section ends at delivering usable camera frames.

slides.title: Replacing ZBar with ZXing-C++
slides.summary: Another AI-assisted library swap: preserve the decoded bytes, change the reader.
points: Compare readers on identical camera frames
Adapt the grayscale input and binary-byte output
Keep animated QR assembly in the application
slides.notes: The existing app used ZBar through pyzbar. AI helped build decoder comparisons, investigate preprocessing, cross-compile ZXing-C++ and connect the native worker to the app. The shared pipeline tried a raw frame, a center crop and finally local thresholding. On the same four saved VGA camera frames, repeated six times each, both pipelines reached 24/24 matching reads. ZXing succeeded on the raw frames; ZBar needed the final threshold stage. Median complete prototype pipeline time was 35.1 ms for ZXing and 174.8 ms for ZBar. This includes preprocessing, process startup and I/O, with capture stopped; it is not live app FPS or a universal decoder ranking. The final threshold helper uses ZXing’s HybridBinarizer, so the successful ZBar pipeline also depends on that preprocessing component. Binary fixtures passed 9/9 for each reader, including NUL and all 256 byte values. The adaptation must preserve bytes rather than force text decoding. Python continues to assemble animated QR formats and interpret application payloads. The QR algorithm itself was not rewritten in Rust.

slides.title: Moving the interface to LVGL
slides.summary: Build on Keith’s longstanding work bringing SeedSigner’s interface to LVGL for microcontrollers.
points: LVGL provides graphics and widgets for embedded devices
Adapt Keith’s screens to the Luckfox Linux platform
Use AI to integrate, test behavior and investigate memory
slides.notes: Keith (kdmukai) has longstanding work porting SeedSigner interfaces to LVGL for microcontrollers. Make that foundation explicit before describing our contribution. LVGL supplies embedded graphics and widgets. We adapted Keith’s screen work to the Luckfox Linux platform and connected it to the existing Python application. AI helped map screen contracts, integrate the native renderer, preserve input/navigation behavior, audit dependencies and measure memory. The Python Controller and models still manage application and wallet logic. The tested development image booted with usable menus and camera scanning on the standard bench hardware. Memory comparisons must account for the same workload and all processes, including Python, the camera, QR worker and renderer. Pillow still has still-image and entropy consumers. Credit SeedSigner, ShieldSigner and Keith’s portable screens; this is adaptation and integration built on their work. The next slide demonstrates those pieces together.

slides.title: Try the camera and interface together
slides.summary: A short demonstration on the working Luckfox bench device.
points: Navigate the LVGL menus with the buttons
Open the camera and scan a public test QR
Return to the menu and repeat the scan
slides.notes: The PCB and enclosure have already been shown; use this section to demonstrate the firmware behavior just discussed. On the prepared Luckfox bench device, navigate the LVGL interface, enter camera scanning, scan a non-secret public test QR in a format the app supports, then leave and enter the scanner again. Explain what is visible rather than claiming broader wallet coverage from a QR scan. The bench uses the standard 240×240 display/button board; the new 2.8-inch carrier still needs first-article qualification. If the device is unavailable, explain the recorded test scope using the linked firmware status rather than presenting the case render as working hardware. Keep seeds, recovery phrases and private wallet data off the projector.

slides.title: What we have verified
slides.summary: Software checks, bench results and remaining carrier tests.
points: Native checks + provenance
Continuity + rails + actual pinmux
Tested bench ≠ qualified carrier
slides.notes: The biggest concrete lesson: the working base-fork firmware drives GPIO56/57 as LCD outputs, while the carrier uses those nets for Left/Up buttons to ground. Pressing a button can ground a driven output. The carrier net map agrees with its intended carrier profile; rewiring it to mimic the bench would be the wrong response. The new carrier needs the carrier image, 10 MHz LCD clock, 320×240 settings and physical bring-up. Frozen-image hashes and packed checks establish exact artifacts, while first-article electrical/mechanical tests establish different facts. AI accelerated finding this mismatch; it did not exempt us from checking it.

Shipping, tax, battery and card excluded

slides.title: Next: assemble and test the carrier
slides.summary: Check the real board, fit the case and verify the complete workflow.
points: Qualify the carrier first article
Practice recovery with disposable keys
Contribute a reproducible improvement
slides.notes: Close with the actual next step: one powered carrier first article with the correct profile, continuity/rail/button/display/camera checks, and a printed fit test. Real-wallet end-to-end acceptance remains pending. Invite review of a net, a footprint, a source guard, an enclosure clearance or a repeatable test rather than generic trust in the prototype. Thank SeedSigner, ShieldSigner, kdmukai/LVGL, Linux, Luckfox and the wider open-source contributors. Link the project and Denver.space. The useful artifact is not only a board: it is a workflow that makes the next question cheaper to answer.
